title: IP and MAC Addresses
intro: An independent 10–15 minute catch-up with feedback, unlimited retries and 80% mastery.

questions.prompt: What does a server do in a client-server network?
What is an IP address used for?
options: Identifying a destination for routing across networks
questions.answer: Identifying a destination for routing across networks

stages.label: Learn
stages.lead: Read and follow the new material.

blocks.title: IP addresses
blocks.text: An IP address identifies a network destination and allows routers to forward traffic between networks. IPv4 is commonly shown as four decimal numbers.

blocks.title: MAC addresses
blocks.text: A MAC address identifies a network interface; it is commonly shown as six pairs of hexadecimal digits.

blocks.title: Switch and router jobs
blocks.text: Within a LAN, switches forward based on MAC addresses. Between networks, routers use IP addresses.

blocks.title: Compare examples
blocks.text: IPv4 and MAC addresses have different roles and formats. Do not confuse a device's IP address with the MAC address of its NIC.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: The computer first communicates on its local network, then needs to reach a remote network. Local network interfaces use MAC addresses [1], allowing switching towards the local gateway [1]. Routers use IP addresses [1] to forward data between networks towards the destination [1]. Match four points to local MAC use and remote IP routing.

items: IP address — Network address used to identify and route to a destination.
IPv4 — A 32-bit IP addressing format typically written as four decimal octets.
IPv6 — A larger IP addressing format written using hexadecimal groups.
MAC address — An address identifying a network interface, typically six hexadecimal pairs.
Switch — Local network device using MAC addresses for forwarding.
Router — Device using IP addresses to route between networks.
